{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in measure theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Cramér–Wold theorem'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Samanta |first=M. |date=1989-04-01 |title=Non-parametric estimation of conditional quantiles |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0167715289900953 |journal=Statistics & Probability Letters |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=407–412 |doi=10.1016/0167-7152(89)90095-3 |issn=0167-7152|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cuesta-Albertos |first1=Juan Antonio |last2=Fraiman |first2=Ricardo |last3=Ransford |first3=Thomas |date=2007 |title=A Sharp Form of the Cramér–Wold Theorem |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10959-007-0060-7 |journal=Journal of Theoretical Probability |language=en |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=201–209 |doi=10.1007/s10959-007-0060-7 |issn=0894-9840|hdl=10908/494 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> or the '''Cramér–Wold device'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mueller |first1=Jonas W |last2=Jaakkola |first2=Tommi |date=2015 |title=Principal Differences Analysis: Interpretable Characterization of Differences between Distributions |url=https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2015/hash/83fa5a432ae55c253d0e60dbfa716723-Abstract.html |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |publisher=Curran Associates, Inc. |volume=28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berger |first1=David |last2=Lindner |first2=Alexander |date=2022-05-01 |title=A Cramér–Wold device for infinite divisibility of Zd-valued distributions |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bernoulli/volume-28/issue-2/A-Cram%c3%a9rWold-device-for-infinite-divisibility-of-Zd-valued-distributions/10.3150/21-BEJ1386.full |journal=Bernoulli |volume=28 |issue=2 |doi=10.3150/21-BEJ1386 |issn=1350-7265|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a theorem in [[measure theory]] and  which states that a [[Borel measure|Borel]] [[probability measure]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^k</math> is uniquely determined by the totality of its one-dimensional projections.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cramér-Wold theorem |url=https://planetmath.org/cramerwoldtheorem |website=planetmath.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Billingsley | first = Patrick | author-link1=Patrick Billingsley| year = 1995 | title = Probability and Measure | edition=3| publisher = [[John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn = 978-0-471-00710-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bélisle |first1=Claude |last2=Massé |first2=Jean-Claude |last3=Ransford |first3=Thomas |date=1997 |title=When is a probability measure determined by infinitely many projections? |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-probability/volume-25/issue-2/When-is-a-probability-measure-determined-by-infinitely-many-projections/10.1214/aop/1024404418.full |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=25 |issue=2 |doi=10.1214/aop/1024404418 |issn=0091-1798}}</ref> It is used as a method for proving joint convergence results. The theorem is named after [[Harald Cramér]] and [[Herman Ole Andreas Wold]], who published the result in 1936.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cramér |first1=H. |last2=Wold |first2=H. |date=1936 |title=Some Theorems on Distribution Functions |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/jlms/s1-11.4.290 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s1-11 |issue=4 |pages=290–294 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-11.4.290|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Let
:<math> {X}_n = (X_{n1},\dots,X_{nk}) </math> 
and
:<math> \; {X} = (X_1,\dots,X_k) </math>
be [[random vector]]s of dimension&nbsp;''k''. Then <math> {X}_n </math> [[Convergence_of_random_variables#Convergence_in_distribution|converges in distribution]] to <math> {X} </math> if and only if:

:<math> \sum_{i=1}^k t_iX_{ni} \overset{D}{\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\rightarrow}} \sum_{i=1}^k t_iX_i. </math> 

for each <math> (t_1,\dots,t_k)\in \mathbb{R}^k </math>, that is, if every fixed [[linear combination]] of the coordinates of <math> {X}_n</math> converges in distribution to the correspondent linear combination of coordinates of <math> {X} </math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Billingsley|1995|page=383}}</ref>

If <math> {X}_n </math> takes values in <math>\mathbb{R}_+^k</math>, then the statement is also true with <math> (t_1,\dots,t_k)\in \mathbb{R}_+^k </math>.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Kallenberg|first=Olav|title=Foundations of modern probability|date=2002|publisher=Springer|isbn=0-387-94957-7|edition=2nd|location=New York|oclc=46937587}}</ref>
